  How rpf() chooses the number of splits out of bag while the forest grows,

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  fig.width = 7,
  fig.height = 4,
  out.width = "100%"
)
```

The main setting of a random planted forest is the number of splits each tree family makes, `n_splits`.
Too few, and the model misses structure; too many, and it fits the noise.
By default `rpf()` chooses it out of bag while the forest grows, in the same call, so it need not be tuned.
This article shows how that works, and how to tune the other settings of the split search.

```{r setup}
library(randomPlantedForest)
```

We use simulated data with two main effects, a two-way and a three-way interaction, and a test set from the same distribution:

```{r simulate}
make_data <- function(n) {
  d <- data.frame(matrix(runif(n * 5, -1, 1), ncol = 5, dimnames = list(NULL, paste0("x", 1:5))))
  d$y <- sin(pi * d$x1) + d$x2 + 2 * d$x1 * d$x3 + 3 * d$x2 * d$x3 * d$x4 + rnorm(n, sd = 0.3)
  d
}
set.seed(3)
train <- make_data(1000)
test <- make_data(2000)
```

## The out-of-bag error

Every tree family is grown on a bootstrap sample of the training rows.
About 37% of the rows are not in a given sample: they are out of bag (OOB) for that family.
A row's OOB prediction is the mean over the families it is out of bag for, so it is a prediction from families that never saw the row, and the error of these predictions estimates the error on new data, without a test set or cross-validation.

The OOB prediction averages only about 37% of the families, so it varies more than the forest's prediction, and the plain OOB error overstates the forest's error.
`rpf()` corrects for this: it estimates each row's variance across families from the families of even and of odd index, and subtracts the excess (`?rpf`, "The out-of-bag path").

One fit gives the OOB error at every number of splits.
With the same seed, the forest with `k` splits is exactly the first `k` splits of a forest grown with more, so each family's OOB predictions are updated split by split while it grows.
`oob_path = TRUE` records them at checkpoints, four per doubling of the splits (`oob_path_checkpoints()`):

```{r path}
set.seed(10)
fixed <- rpf(y ~ ., data = train, n_families = 50, n_splits = 1600, oob_path = TRUE,
             prune = FALSE, nthreads = 2)
head(fixed$oob_path)
```

To check the OOB error against the test error, we grow the same forest (same seed) to several of the checkpoints and compute its error on the test set:

```{r path-vs-test, fig.alt = "Plain and corrected out-of-bag error against the number of splits on a log scale, with the test error at eight checkpoints."}
ks <- c(12, 25, 50, 100, 200, 400, 800, 1600)
test_rmse <- sapply(ks, function(k) {
  set.seed(10)
  f <- rpf(y ~ ., data = train, n_families = 50, n_splits = k, prune = FALSE, nthreads = 2)
  sqrt(mean((test$y - predict(f, test)$.pred)^2))
})

path <- fixed$oob_path
plot(path$n_splits, path$oob_rmse_raw, log = "x", type = "l", lty = 2,
     ylim = range(path$oob_rmse, path$oob_rmse_raw, test_rmse),
     xlab = "splits per family", ylab = "RMSE")
lines(path$n_splits, path$oob_rmse)
points(ks, test_rmse, pch = 19, col = "orange")
legend("topright", c("OOB, plain", "OOB, corrected", "test set"), lty = c(2, 1, NA),
       pch = c(NA, NA, 19), col = c("black", "black", "orange"), bty = "n")
```

The corrected OOB error follows the test error; the plain one lies above it.
Both fall steeply and then flatten: past some number of splits, more splits buy nothing but time.
Choosing `n_splits` by the corrected OOB error usually does as well as cross-validation over the same values.

## The default: `n_splits = NULL`

With `n_splits = NULL`, `rpf()` follows the forest's corrected OOB error checkpoint by checkpoint while the families grow, and stops growing once more splits no longer help:

- once the lowest error is one doubling of the splits back (for example, no new minimum from 100 to 200 splits), or
- once the error is on a plateau: its lowest value improved over the last doubling by at most one standard error of that improvement.

The forest at the lowest error is returned: the same forest that `rpf()` with that number of splits and the same seed would give.
Growing also stops at 25,600 splits, with a warning if the error was still falling there.

```{r default}
set.seed(10)
model <- rpf(y ~ ., data = train, nthreads = 2)
model$fit$splits_oob
```

`n_splits` is the chosen number of splits and `stopped_at` where growing stopped; `capped` says whether it stopped at 25,600 with the error still falling.
The path of the checkpoints grown is in `model$fit$oob_path`:

```{r default-path, fig.alt = "Corrected out-of-bag error at each checkpoint grown by the default call, with the chosen number of splits marked."}
path <- model$fit$oob_path
plot(path$n_splits, path$oob_rmse, log = "x", type = "b", pch = 20,
     xlab = "splits per family", ylab = "corrected OOB RMSE")
abline(v = model$fit$splits_oob$n_splits, col = "orange")
```

The families do not all grow to the end and wait: they grow one at a time (`nthreads` at once), each to the stop estimated from the families before it, and keep only their OOB predictions and a short record of their splits, from which the chosen forest is rebuilt.
This keeps the memory of the search small; [Speed and memory](speed-and-memory.html) says more.

The plateau stop's tolerance is `getOption("randomPlantedForest.adaptive_tolerance", 1)`, in standard errors.
`0` stops only on the first rule.


## A fixed number of splits

`n_splits = <number>` grows every family to that many splits.
`oob_path = TRUE` with a fixed `n_splits` gives the path above but stops according to `n_splits`.

A "split" counts a round of the search: a round tries its candidates and makes the best split, and near saturation, when every candidate's leaf is too small to split, a round can make none.

## Tuning the split search: `tune`

The number of splits is chosen in every fit.
Two other settings matter on some data: the greediness of the split search (`n_try_split_points` and `share_candidates`, see [How the forest is grown](growing.html)) and the minimum leaf size `min_leaf_rows`.
`rpf(tune = )` searches them out of bag in one call: every forest of the search gets its number of splits chosen out of bag and is pruned, and the forest whose pruned model has the lowest corrected OOB error wins.

- `tune = "quick"` grows two forests: 3 / 0.1 (the default) and 1 / 0.025.
- `tune = TRUE` runs a coordinate search of about 10 forests: the greediness ladder from 10 / 0.4 to 1 / 0.0125 at `min_leaf_rows = 1`, then `min_leaf_rows` 1, 5, 20 and 100 at the chosen point, then the two neighbours of the chosen point on the ladder.
- `tune = tune_control(...)` sets your own search (see below).

```{r ladder}
greediness_ladder()
```

```{r tune}
set.seed(10)
tuned <- rpf(y ~ ., data = train, tune = "quick", nthreads = 2)
tuned$tune$search[, c("n_try_split_points", "share_candidates", "min_leaf_rows",
                      "n_splits", "n_kept", "oob_rmse", "final")]
tuned$tune$settings
```

The result is the chosen forest's pruned model, with the search in `$tune`.
A search costs about as many fits as it grows forests.

### Your own search: `tune_control()`

`tune_control()` has four arguments, one for each part of the search:

- `ladder`: the points of greediness that can be searched, greediest first. The default is `greediness_ladder()`, shown above; you can pass your own data frame with the columns `n_try_split_points` and `share_candidates`.
- `search`: the rows of the ladder that are tried in the first step (default `3:8`, from 10 / 0.4 to 1 / 0.0125).
- `min_leaf_rows`: the leaf sizes tried in the second step, at the point of greediness chosen in the first (default `c(1, 5, 20, 100)`). The first value is the one used in the first step. With a single value the second step is skipped.
- `neighbours`: whether a third step also tries the two ladder points next to the chosen one (default `TRUE`).

So `tune = TRUE` is `tune_control()` with its defaults, and `tune = "quick"` is `tune_control(search = c(5, 7), min_leaf_rows = 1, neighbours = FALSE)`.

A search of your own is useful when you already know where to look, or when a fit is expensive and you want few forests.
Here we try three points of greediness and then two leaf sizes, four forests in all:

```{r tune-control}
set.seed(10)
own <- rpf(
  y ~ .,
  data = train,
  tune = tune_control(search = c(3, 5, 7), min_leaf_rows = c(1, 20), neighbours = FALSE),
  nthreads = 2
)
own$tune$search[, c("n_try_split_points", "share_candidates", "min_leaf_rows",
                    "n_splits", "n_kept", "oob_rmse", "final")]
```

Each row is one forest of the search, and `final` marks the chosen one.


Usually the accuracy is already very good with the defaults. But tuning can give some additional boost in accuracy.
